:::{#thm-svd}
#### Singular value decomposition

Let $\matr{A}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix with real entries
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r$ (@def-rank).
Then there are
an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{U}$,
a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{V}$ (@def-orthogonal-matrix),
and numbers $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r > 0$
such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{n \times p}
= \underbrace{\matr{U}}_{n \times n}\,
\underbrace{\matr{D}}_{n \times p}\,
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{V}}}_{p \times p}
$$

where $\matr{D}$ has entries $d_{ii} = \sigma_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, r$
and every other entry $0$.
The numbers $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r$ are the **singular values** of $\matr{A}$,
and $\matr{U}\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}$ is a
**singular value decomposition** (SVD) of $\matr{A}$.

:::

::: notes
The proof is outside the scope of these notes;
see @banerjee2014linear [Chapter 12, Theorem 12.1, p. 373].
Unlike the spectral theorem (@thm-spectral),
the SVD applies to every real matrix,
including one that is not square or not symmetric.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-svd}
#### The SVD of a $3 \times 2$ matrix

Let

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{U} = \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\matr{V} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The columns of $\matr{U}$ are orthonormal,
and $\matr{V}$ is the orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ from @exm-spectral,
so $\matr{U}$ and $\matr{V}$ are orthogonal.
$\matr{V}$ is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{V}} = \matr{V}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute; move the scalar to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ \sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(divide by } \sqrt{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

and

$$
\ba
\matr{U}\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 + 0 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 + 0 \\
0 + 1 + 0 & 0 - 1 + 0 \\
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 - 0 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} + 0 - 0
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

which is $\matr{A}$.
$\matr{A}$ has rank $2$, because its two columns are linearly independent,
and its singular values are $\sigma_1 = 2$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{2}$.

:::
